V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00443

As Ruzbihan writes: “There is only one and the same love, and it is in the book of human love (ishq insani) that we must learn to read the rule of divine love (ishq rabbani).” It is, then, one and the same text, but we must learn to read it. Here, above all, interpreting the text turns out to mean interpreting the soul itself.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00444

We must be initiated into a spiritual way of interpretation, a ta'wil of love, because human love is a prophetic text. That means it has a double meaning, an ambiguity or overlap of meanings—the iltibas that Ruzbihan made a technical term of his teaching.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00445

And since Beauty is the source of the text, discovering that source is itself a prophetic act: the mystical lover is a partner of the Prophet (Nabi). Conversely, the message borne by beauty is prophetic. It invites us to pass from figurative love (majazi)—the literal text, love as experienced through the senses—to love in its true sense (haqiqi), the inner meaning of love. These terms are all familiar from the classical Sufi teaching on love, whose defining movement is precisely this passage from figurative meaning to true meaning.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00446

Here again, Ruzbihan's life gives us a concrete example. Ibn Arabi relates a remarkable story from one of Ruzbihan's stays in Mecca. If we set it beside the autobiographical prologue to the Jasmine, the two accounts shed light on one another. Ibn Arabi had heard the story in the Sufi circles of Mecca, where it must have been well known, and included it in a chapter of his vast work, The Meccan Spiritual Conquests.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00447

During what was probably an extended stay in the holy city, Ruzbihan fell in love with a beautiful young singer. In a man like Ruzbihan, such love could take only one form: adoring love carried to the point of ecstasy. A characteristic feature of his devotions and ecstatic states, as the Diary also shows, was that he sighed and cried out aloud, sometimes to the point of disturbing those worshipping near him. This was exactly what happened in Mecca, where his exclamations disturbed others walking around the Kaaba in the ritual circumambulation.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00448

Ibn Arabi also attests that Ruzbihan was a man of complete inner sincerity. We have already recognized in him the traits that connect him with the Malamati: those fearless people who, precisely to remain completely faithful to their own inner truth, do not shrink from public blame. Whatever image nourished his ecstasy, its outward manifestations remained the same.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00449

Because no one knew of his love, Ruzbihan sensed that people might misunderstand him. They might suppose that his ecstasies still arose from God alone, as they had before. Or, rather, he must have realized that the people around him could not even imagine the experience he would later describe in the Jasmine: for the pious ascetics, divine love and human love were irreconcilable opposites.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00450

So, with the fearless simplicity of a pure heart, Ruzbihan went before the assembly of Sufis. There he took off his khirqa, his Sufi cloak, threw it down before his companions, told them what had happened, and concluded: “I do not want to lie to anyone about my state.” From that moment he devoted himself entirely to this young beauty of Mecca.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00451

But we must look closely at what he did. Ruzbihan was behaving as a true member of the faithful in love. This was no ordinary “affair,” as we might say today. Ruzbihan kept his secret; in silence, his ecstasy was nourished by the vision of her beauty. Others told the young woman that she was the unknowing object of ecstatic adoration by someone already regarded as one of the great spiritual figures (min akabir ahl Allah).
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00452

What happened then was this. The news deeply moved her. Overwhelmed, she renounced the way of life she had followed until then and turned toward God. Ibn Arabi says that her conversion was the blessed fruit of Ruzbihan's sincerity. She became his disciple in turn, just as Ruzbihan had been hers: contemplating her beauty had led him to the point where the mystic ceases to be attached to outward form.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00453

The outcome perfectly reflects the ethic of the faithful in love. The beautiful person who receives this adoration is ultimately transformed by it. The lover invests her with a theophanic role—the role of revealing the divine—and this leads her to the inner truth of her beauty, a truth henceforth beyond the changes of time. The story ends with a gesture just as simple as the first. Ruzbihan returns to the Sufi assembly and takes up his khirqa again.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00454

Comparing this moving and revealing story with the opening chapter of the book Ruzbihan called The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love, we cannot help noticing certain parallels. From the autobiographical details in that prologue, we learn that when Ruzbihan set out to write the book, he had already reached a high degree of spiritual advancement.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00455

But he still had to undergo the trial of love. That meant being initiated into his own distinctive form of spirituality: one that experiences human love not as a temptation to conquer, as ordinary ascetics do, but as a summons to spiritual transformation. Upon this transformation depends access to inward tawhid: the discovery that one and the same being is love, lover, and beloved.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00456

All of this agrees with the situation described in the prologue to the Jasmine, and with the teaching it promises to unfold: “With the eyes of the heart I contemplated uncreated Beauty; with the eyes of the intellect I sought to understand the secret of the human form.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00457

The prologue is itself a spiritual autobiography. Through images and allusions, it describes the point Ruzbihan had reached on the spiritual path when his progress was to be tested through love. I have translated the prologue elsewhere, so I will quote only a few passages here: “Having returned from the heavenly world, what I experienced in this world was the very condition of being put to the test: the desolation of finding and yet not finding (the feeling that what one has attained remains inaccessible even in the moment of attainment). It was then that I made my home in the world of Beauty [...].
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00458

“Consumed by this loving melancholy for divine Beauty, I migrated into the passing world of created beings. My destiny carried me toward the company of beautiful people [...]. And suddenly, at the edge of the Square of Bounties, in the mirror of the Signs of beauty, I perceived the divine Attributes.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00459

Then, just as in Mecca—to such a degree that we are tempted to wonder whether one event has been transposed into the other—a beautiful being suddenly appears before a man already far advanced on the inward Way. Ruzbihan leaves her identity vague, referring to her simply as a “charming fairy” (jinni lo'bati) or a “heavenly maiden,” although he draws on every resource of the Persian language to describe her extraordinary beauty.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00460

The moment of her appearance is precisely located on the horizon of his soul's inner time. He has just recalled meditating upon two Quranic verses that are among the sacred “texts” of the mystical devotion to human beauty: “We created the human being in the most beautiful of forms” (95:4); “Oh, how beautiful is your form!” (40:66; 64:3). This is the moment when the revelation of human beauty floods Ruzbihan's consciousness in the way that a Sufi experiences it: at once an enchantment of joy and a kind of sacred dread before the very secret of the divine within the human. To encounter beauty face to face is therefore to suffer the torment of finding and not finding.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00461

Our modern civilizations have so thoroughly “desacralized” human beauty—through metaphysical secularization following upon religious asceticism, through unconscious profanations committed in the name of advertising or sporting conventions, and through supposedly enlightened “demythologizations”—that the numinous, or awe-inspiring sacred, character beauty possesses for the faithful in love may be among the strangest, most alien things imaginable to a person today.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00462

Yet this is as fundamental a phenomenon (Urphänomen) as perceiving a sound or a color. A sound or a color cannot be “proved.” Either one is able to perceive beauty as at once fascinating and terrifying, awakening joy and desperate longing, bearing witness to a presence that is nevertheless not there and to an absence that nevertheless gives a sign of itself here—as Ruzbihan will describe it—or one is unable to perceive it. In the latter case, it is better not to speak of the religion of the faithful in love at all.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00463

Ruzbihan suddenly sees this beauty before him, leaving us uncertain whether he is describing a vision or a physical encounter. Or rather, he is describing what normally happens in his experience: every event in the visible world opens out into a visionary perception of the invisible. A dialogue then begins, held together by a delicate thread, its alternating exchanges artfully arranged.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00464

We must follow its stages, because they disclose the whole purpose of the book. The opening situation is this. In Mecca, the beautiful young woman initially knew nothing of the mystical adoration directed toward her. Here, the woman who will become the book's dedicatee is no doubt fully aware of her own beauty, but she knows nothing of what that beauty can mean to a Sufi.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00465

To put it technically, she does not understand the theophanic role—the power to reveal the divine—with which her beauty has been endowed. The irony of the dialogue is that she herself takes it upon herself to remind the Sufi Ruzbihan of the orthodox teaching of the “pious ascetics”: to make her beauty an object of contemplation is to go astray.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00466

Ruzbihan greets her with enthusiasm: “You belong to the company of the mystics faithful in love, O beautiful icon! You are supremely worthy of them, even though you do not join us in drinking the wine of love at the gathering of ecstasy.” She answers: “To turn away from the divine world would be a culpable neglect. To make me the object of your contemplation would be the place of your ruin—unless, indeed, you are already lost.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00467

The first episode reveals that this apparent dialogue is really a monologue. Ruzbihan replies: “Many have lost their way in love. Rational intellect has no power, through the treasure of your love, to enter into that other love”—divine love. And he dares to ask: “As you are known to the gaze of God”—that is, as God beholds Himself in you—“who, then, are you? Tell me. And as you are in the secret of the theophanies, what are you?”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00468

The answer rises from Ruzbihan's own consciousness. It is the young woman who is supposed to speak, certainly, but she speaks as she exists in his vision: “She said to me: The secret of divinity (lahut) is within humanity (nasut), without the divinity being disturbed by incarnation. The beauty of the human creature is the direct reflection of divine Beauty. Creation begins with me; it comes to its fulfillment in God.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00469

There follows a short poem that might have flowered on the lips of Sophia, divine Wisdom, in the Book of Wisdom: “You are the appearing of beauty to me, O Beloved! Will you not tell me where your being comes from?—I am the work of the hands of divinity (lahut). I am the leader and guide of humanity (nasut). I was the first creature to exist in the world (...). It is me whom God contemplates through every creature; yet my own nature remains separate from every creature.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00470

Ruzbihan sinks deeper into his inward dialogue: “I perceived the mystery of Beauty in the human image offered me by this bride, in the majesty that made the grace of her essential nature so imposing.... Through prolonged contemplation, the qualities of her soul's purity took on for me an immaterial form (bi-makan, independent of the place where they appeared).” What constituted the essence beneath her outward human form became independent, for him, of its visible symbol.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00471

So independent, indeed, that his charming interlocutor finds the conversation is going on too long and tries to break it off. Still no closer to understanding what she has to do with any of this, she repeats her first thoroughly orthodox warning: “To my mind, Sufism is incompatible with license. Making me the object of contemplation is no business of people who profess the spiritual life (ahl-e walayat).”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00472

In short, the “charming fairy” speaks with an orthodoxy that neither Qushayri nor Ibn Taymiyya would disown. The contemplative should contemplate the Creator's power in His work. There is no place for emotion in that.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00473

Now the questions alternate, becoming more urgent and more decisive. “After all this, she spoke again to test me: ‘O Sufi! What place does human love have in divine love?’—I said to her: ‘The love I feel for you is precisely the beginning of that divine love.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00474

“The condition of iltibas—the double meaning in which one reality appears through another—is absolutely unavoidable if one is to experience the ecstatic intoxication of divine love, whether one is a beginner or the most accomplished of mystics.’—She: ‘On the path you follow, to feel love for me can only be an error.’—I: ‘The Book revealed to our Prophet itself bears witness to chaste love.’”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00475

Ruzbihan invokes in support the magnificent twelfth surah of the Quran, the story of Joseph. He adds traditions handed down from the Prophet, among them one especially dear to the faithful in love: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies without betraying his secret, dies as a true witness (shahid, ‘martyr’).” Or this one: “Whoever is possessed by love and an overwhelming preoccupation with God, for God and in God, loves beautiful faces.” And there are all the sayings of the Sufi masters, such as this one from Dhu'l-Nun al-Misri: “Whoever has become intimate with God is intimate with every beautiful thing and every graceful face.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00476

These are impressive authorities, and Ruzbihan could multiply them. (He might have referred to Suhrawardi's Vade Mecum of the Faithful in Love, had he known it.) Beneath their densely allusive language lies the decisive question for the faithful in love: what does it mean to love God? Whom does the mystic love when he speaks of his love for God? Can one love a being of whom one has no image or conception at all?
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00477

But if an image is needed, where can it arise, and from what? In the absence of such an image, is it even legitimate to use the word love in speaking of God? Ruzbihan's beautiful interlocutor, whose stern orthodoxy seems to be wavering, now asks: “Tell me, is it permissible to use the word love (ishq, eros) of God? May anyone claim to love Him with passionate love? Is the word love, as mystics use it, merely a homonym—a word that has different meanings in different contexts? Are we permitted to speak of love in relation to God: love of God, in God, through God?”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00478

This question is so important that it not only defines where Sufism stands in relation to the monotheism of outward Islam; it has also divided the Sufi masters themselves. Ruzbihan replies at length, invoking those who allow such language.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00479

After all, was David not said to have been called “the passionate lover of God” (ashiq Allah)? And did certain members of the Quraysh not declare, “Truly, Muhammad has fallen in love with his God”? For Ruzbihan, the fact that such love is attested in the person of the Prophet carries more weight than all the arguments proving that one may legitimately love God. For the Prophet Muhammad, the model of prophetic Sufism, had seen his God “in the most beautiful of forms.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00480

Ruzbihan then recalls the celebrated pairs of lovers in Arabic and Persian courtly poetry. He goes back as far as the Prophet's own circle, to Bishr and Hind, and recalls the Prophet's moving words about them: “Glory be to God, who has raised up within my community rivals to Joseph and Zulaykha!”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00481

“Moreover,” he continues, “it was of human love as the royal road to divine love that these words were spoken: Be chaste before God, and keep hidden in your soul what He causes to blossom there (33:37).... Read again the books that preserve the memories of the prophets, and understand that we are not concerned here with theoretical reflections on love.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00482

“As for divine love, we cannot cross the rushing river—the Jayhun—of tawhid without first crossing the bridge of your love. The prophets and the spiritual friends of God (Awliya) are protected from suspicions of carnal desire. This is the subtle point in love that those versed in iltibas, in its double meaning, know so well.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00483
At the end of this prologue, which so clearly announces the book's purpose, we encounter once again this characteristic term from Ruzbihan's vocabulary.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00484
We can now begin to grasp what it means for a teaching that will present the experience of human love as initiation into inward tawhid.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00485

We can also appreciate the concise definition Ruzbihan gives elsewhere: “The beginnings of divine love require human reality (bandagi); the sublimity of tawhid requires divine reality (khoda'i). It is this situation that I have named iltibas, the overlap of meanings.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00486

Now Ruzbihan's interlocutor is shaken. Is he not revealing her to herself by revealing the meaning of the beauty she bears, the beauty that makes him her disciple, one of her faithful in love? The roles become reciprocal, just as they did in Mecca when the beautiful singer became Ruzbihan's disciple in turn.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00487

“By God!” she asks, “could you explain to me in Persian how human love is involved in divine love? Could you write a little book that would serve as a spiritual guide—an Imam—for us, and for all lovers and beloveds, a subject of meditation for pilgrims devoted to the religion of love?”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00488

Ruzbihan hastens to fulfill his beloved's wish, to obey her command: “And so I began to compose a book to make human and divine love clear, that it might bring lovers and the faithful in love the joy of intimacy, the flowers of the most holy Paradise. I have called it The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00489

The book's governing intention, and the occasion that gave rise to it, have now been set out. Ruzbihan will write in the inward presence of the woman to whom it is dedicated. That presence is recalled at the end of each chapter in a kind of lyrical psalm evoking the power of her beauty to reveal the divine.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00490

Together, the book's thirty-two chapters trace the route of an inward pilgrimage. Here we can mention only its major stages. We already possess some of its essential ideas and terms. We have just dwelt on iltibas, the overlap or ambiguity of meanings, a term we have met several times because it is inseparable from the idea governing all Ruzbihan's Sufism: theophany (tajalli, zohur), the manifestation of the divine.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00491

From that idea follows his understanding of how the divine and the human are related, and how such a relationship is possible. From it follows, in turn, the idea that human love can initiate us into inward tawhid. This stands in the sharpest possible contrast to habits of thought inherited elsewhere from a negative asceticism, so alien to the vision of the faithful in love that their teaching appears to it as a paradox.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00492

The idea of theophany itself calls for another key term, already found in the Book of the Clouding and frequently used in the Jasmine. It is one of the essential words in the vocabulary of all those spiritual teachers who have professed the religion of mystical love for the supreme divine Attribute, Beauty—the manifestation of the divine in beauty. That word is shahid. It is difficult to translate with a single English term. Its Arabic root, from which it forms the word for the person performing an action, conveys the ideas of being personally present at an event, witnessing it with one's own eyes, and testifying to what one has seen.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00493

Thus shahid can mean “one who is present,” “one who contemplates,” or “witness.” The Sufis also use it for a psychological phenomenon: the inward image of something absent, which the image makes present, or even any content of consciousness that predominates at a given moment. In a more specialized sense, finally, they mean by it any beautiful person one loves, either because that person's beauty makes present and bears witness to distant, absent, invisible divine Beauty—re-presents it—or because one carries that person's image within one's heart.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00494

The shahid, then, is the beautiful face the mystic takes as a “witness of contemplation,” whether in inward imagination, during the sama or spiritual concert, or in a personal encounter. Insofar as the beautiful person bears witness to invisible Beauty, making it present and visible, this person is a witness who testifies.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00495

But at the very same time, the beauty of the witness is the object of the mystic's contemplation. The shahid—the one who performs the witnessing—is also the mashhud: the one contemplated, the one attested to, the one made present. The word thus has two meanings and performs two functions. We believe both are best conveyed by “witness of contemplation”: active and passive, subject and object. The witness is a subject who calls forth contemplation by bearing witness and by being present; and precisely in doing so, the witness also becomes the object of that contemplation.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00496

This double meaning becomes fully intelligible at the level of inward tawhid, the consciousness the initiate must ultimately attain. We need only turn to the mystical commentaries on the Quranic verse (85:3, the surah of the Zodiac), where the two words appear together in a mysterious oath. They are interpreted through the idea that God is at once love, lover, and beloved.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00497

Ruzbihan declares, for example: “The shahid is He, and the mashhud is He. He sees Himself through Himself, for in truth no one sees Him.... The shahid is He, and the mashhud is the hearts of the mystics to whom He is present”—that is, He is their shahid precisely by being their mashhud: it is He who contemplates them when they contemplate Him—“and the shahid is also the hearts of the mystical lovers, while their mashhud is having Him face to face. He is their shahid and He is their mashhud. He is the gnostic's shahid, and, in return, the gnostic is His shahid.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00498

This is why Ruzbihan's understanding of shahid, with the reciprocity and reversibility belonging to the “witness of contemplation”—the one who both contemplates and is contemplated—is inseparable from the image of a mirror. Our spiritual writers constantly turn to the mirror to explain what inward knowledge involves. The mirror, in turn, holds the secret of theophany (tajalli), the appearing of the divine.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00499

We are dealing with a whole network of images and ideas, each closely bound to the others. Understood as something like a reflection in a mirror, theophany distinguishes Sufism both from the monotheism of Islamic orthodoxy and from the Christian orthodox doctrine of incarnation. Precisely because it works like a mirror, theophany allows us to conceive the mystery within the divine itself—the identity of love, lover, and beloved—and enables the mystic to glimpse and experience it.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00500

The idea of theophany reveals Sufism's enduring kinship with Shiism, just as it marks Sufism off from every abstract monotheism. It involves the idea of divine anthropomorphosis: the divine taking the appearance of human form. The Human Form, the heavenly Anthropos, the spiritual Adam, is the manifestation of God. This human form is at once the shahid that contemplates God and shows God His own Image, and, in showing that Image to Him, also becomes His mashhud—the Image He contemplates. It is through this form that God becomes visible.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00501

It makes possible the prophetic affirmation: “I contemplated my God in the most beautiful of forms.” This vision stands midway between tashbih, making God resemble created things, and ta'til, stripping divinity of its qualities until nothing remains but an abstraction. These are the two dangers that threaten abstract monotheism, into one or the other of which it falls when it lacks the help of theophany. (The whole Shiite understanding of the Imams rests upon this insight.)
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00502
Yet this is also what distinguishes Sufi theosophy from the dogma of the Incarnation defined by the Christian councils.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00503

What is at issue is a taking of human form on the heavenly plane, in the Malakut, the angelic fullness of being—not an irreversible historical event on earth in which divinity enters human clay, human “flesh.” It is not with their bodily eyes that witnesses behold this theophany in “history.” They behold it “in Heaven,” through the faculty of heavenly sight (chashm-e malakuti), as caro spiritualis, spiritual flesh.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00504

And because it is an “event in Heaven,” not a material occurrence irrevocably fixed in history, the theophany can be repeated as often as a shahid is present—as often as a beautiful face is invested with its prophetic meaning. It is neither enôikêsis (holûl, indwelling or immanence) nor ensarkosis (tajassod, incarnation). Nor is it kenosis, an emptying, exhaustion, or withdrawal of the divine. It is the triumphant manifestation, radiant with majesty, of the divine Attribute above all others: Beauty.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00505

Every renewal of this heavenly event gives rise to the ecstatic devotion to Beauty. To reject beauty, as do the various forms of asceticism—in religion, art, or social life—is a sacrilegious betrayal on humanity's part. In so doing, humanity takes it upon itself to drive God out of Paradise. For beauty is the very way of being of Paradise: to see it, and truly understand what it announces, is to enter that way of being. Adam—that is, human beauty—is the shahid, and Paradise is the mashhad, the place of this witnessing, this Presence.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00506

The mystery of this mashhad is what every comparison with a mirror tries to make clear. God does not become incarnate: divine Beauty “enters into” beautiful forms as an image “enters” a mirror. The earthly human condition cannot be redeemed by dragging the divine down to its own level, but only by the transfiguration the divine brings about within it.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00507

The Image is not incarnated in the mirror. Rather, by appearing there—in that mashhad—it sees and shows to himself the person looking into the mirror, the person whose image it is. The one looking sees himself by means of this image. Without it, he could not see himself. That is why the eye of the Image is the eye through which he sees himself. Ruzbihan has already taught us this.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00508

To look at the image is vision. To see that the gaze of the Image—the gaze of the shahid—is my own gaze looking back at me through that Image: that is the vision of vision. Ultimately, there is a gaze directed upon myself without my own act of looking. It is Majnun's gaze, which is Layla: the secret of the Lover who is the Beloved. These reflections lend support to some of the most striking passages we previously encountered in the Book of the Clouding. It is out of longing for a shahid, a witness, that God creates the world.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00509

Yet the gaze of that witness can only be God's own gaze beholding Himself: the vision of vision. Otherwise God “cannot see it.” And that is why, since its creation, God has not looked upon this eyeless world—a world blind through refusal or unconsciousness.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00510

We can now begin to see why the divine identity of love, lover, and beloved requires the idea of theophany. As with a mirror, theophany consists in God's being both shahid and mashhud: the one who contemplates and the one contemplated. And because the theophany is a manifestation of Beauty, and Beauty's theophany takes human form, it follows that shahid and mashhud have been human beauty—the heavenly Anthropos—since before all beginnings, in the pre-eternity of pre-eternities.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00511

When Ruzbihan's young interlocutor says that the mystic should contemplate the Creator's power in the creature and form an idea of that power from the creature, she is innocently speaking the rational language of cause and effect used by theologians and pious ascetics.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00512

The feeling for theophany among the faithful in love is altogether different. They do not need to start from one thing in order to reach another. They must look directly, face to face. We see an image only in the mirror, not elsewhere, and not by reasoning our way toward it from the mirror. This is the whole basis of human love in the idea of theophany.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00513

Creation is theophany; and as theophany it is anthropomorphosis, the manifestation of God in the heavenly human form (see further below). It follows that from the pre-eternity of Creation there has been a unio mystica, a mystical union, between divinity and the human form. It is this same relation of theophany—the speculative or mirror-like (speculum means “mirror”) foundation of the identity of love, lover, and beloved—that grounds the revelation of divine love in human love.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00514

For at the furthest limit of its mystical experience, human love is precisely this form of divine love. We are reading the one text at last in its true sense, provided that we do not look at the mirror without seeing the image. To do that would still be merely figurative love (ishq majazi).
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00515
We must look instead at the Image appearing in the mirror (ishq haqiqi, love in its true sense), an Image that is your very gaze.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00516

Human love leads us toward inward tawhid because we must pass through the trial of the Veil—the “clouding”—and love alone can make that Veil transparent as a mirror. Majnun is Layla. He knows that it is Layla loving herself through Majnun's love for her.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00517

Majnun has then understood inward tawhid: it is God loving Himself through Majnun's love for Layla's beauty, which reveals God to him. That is why, at its ultimate limit, as we shall see, inward tawhid speaks in the very language of the highest consciousness of human love. It requires a transformation of self-awareness of the kind Ruzbihan describes in his Risala-ye Qodsiya: “The inward meanings of tawhid are not for just anyone who sets out on the Way to discover.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00518

“For the secret of tawhid that must be discovered is the garment covering the divine condition, through which the soul of the soul (the Beloved in the true sense) appears under a double meaning. Until the mystical pilgrim becomes 1 × 1 (wahid dar wahid, not 1 + 1), he cannot attain the vision of vision (iyan-e iyan), which is tawhid.”
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00519
We can now group the themes marking the stages of the inward pilgrimage that the author of the Jasmine invites us to undertake beside him.
V. The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love
passage-en-00520

They are, in broad outline: (1) the idea of theophany as the divine taking human form in the beauty of the human figure; (2) the understanding of Adam that follows from this, which entails a prophetic meaning of beauty, since Beauty is the supreme sacred, religious, and mystical revelation: Muhammad is the prophet of this revelation and of the religion of love it sustains; (3) the discovery of beauty's prophetic meaning by whoever penetrates the secret of iltibas, the double meaning expressed in the mirror; (4) the pre-existent foundation of this recognition in the pre-eternity of the Holy Spirits (arwah-e qodsi), the spiritual identities of human beings existing before their earthly lives; (5) the realization of this prophetic meaning through an interpretation of the soul that passes from contemplating the mirror as an object to contemplating the Image revealed within it as shahid-mashhud, the one contemplating and contemplated—a schooling in love that leads from figurative love (majazi) to love in its true sense (haqiqi); and (6) the discovery, and lived experience, at the furthest perfection of human love, of the secret of inward tawhid: that in the perfection of love, God Himself is love, lover, and beloved. It is here that the “story” of the faithful in love comes to an end.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00521
Chapter VI The Inner Pilgrimage
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00522

The more one reads and rereads The Jasmine of the Faithful in Love, the harder it becomes to place the work within any established literary genre. To follow the movement of its inspiration, one would need to approach it as a piece of music, tracing its themes, counterthemes, responses, transpositions, episodes, and so on. Any attempt to impose a system on it introduces a rational order that conceals its richness.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00523

Almost every chapter returns to the six themes outlined above. They sound through one another, sometimes as hints, sometimes in overlapping voices, carried by a language of incomparable beauty, though so archaic and difficult that even an Iranian reader today finds it challenging. And it is through these recurring notes, now subdued, now resounding, that the inner pilgrimage unfolds, leading ever deeper into the mystery of beauty and the love that initiates us into it.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
en-book-3-ch-6-s1
1. The Theophany in Beauty
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00524

The first theme is the divine assumption of human form: the primordial theophany, or manifestation, of the Divine Being, who is at once love, lover, and beloved. When the creative command fulfilled the desire of the Divine Being to reveal itself in creation, and forms and figures appeared, “it was in the human form that the quintessence of all existence was concentrated, because this form was the most subtle of the essences of the heavenly realm (malakût).”
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00525

Rûzbehân expresses the point in a brief formula, also taken up by his anonymous commentator: “Adam [the heavenly Human Being] is God himself, clothed in the garment of existence (libâs-e hastî) and assuming the human condition [that is, taking on human form].” This theophany was itself the act of an eternal love whose “object” was its own beauty. It necessarily unfolded through the attributes of grace and beauty and passed through successive veils, already described in the Book of the Clouding: Intelligence, Spirit, Heart, and physical nature. These are at once stages of the cosmos and levels of consciousness within the human microcosm.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00526

Qur’anic verses and sayings of the Prophet (hadith) proclaiming the divine beauty of the human form are frequently invoked. Earthly humanity is the veil of physical nature covering the radiant beauty of the One who contemplates and is contemplated (shâhid-mashhûd). For—and this must be stressed again—the divine assumption of human form takes place on a heavenly plane. Adam belongs to the malakût: he is still the angelic Adam.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00527

That is why Rûzbehân repeatedly insists: “Know that the mystery of the theophanic Manifestation is in no way an incarnation. Otherwise, when the divine Essence revealed itself in its theophanies, the majesty of that Essence would be abolished; and these many qiblas [the beautiful faces toward which love turns] would lose their proper function, which is to make direct vision possible within the vision of the theophanies themselves.”
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00528

We must say it plainly: the belief that the divine literally takes material flesh is what leads love astray. It places the first obstacle in the path of the faithful lover, an obstacle that must be crossed and overcome before one can know love as theophany. That knowledge means seeing the Image that appears in the mirror without imagining that it has become part of the mirror’s material substance.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00529

The divine assumption of human form concerns form, not the materiality of “flesh.” When these are confused—by Christians who affirm incarnation and by the jurists (foqahâ’) who condemn it—human Eros is likewise confused with bodily sexuality. Without a genuine sense of theophany, one can never experience human love as Rûzbehân does: as an initiation into the divine love that is itself the source of the divine assumption of human form. Rûzbehân admits that he once faced this obstacle himself.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00530

At first he, too, could not distinguish the immaterial appearance of the Beloved: “He did not yet understand that this event takes place outside human clay, without any material penetration of the divine Attributes within the boundaries of created being, and without anything resembling an emanation of those Attributes beyond those boundaries. Had he understood, he would have sought beyond the realm of created being what cannot be contained or held within it; and with the dew of tears shed in love’s sorrow, he would have wiped the dust of transience from the face of the Eternal Bride.”
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00531

To “wipe away this dust” is to perceive the theophany where it appears—in its place of manifestation, its mazhar—while recognizing that the eternal Image remains, as it were, suspended there, not physically incorporated into or confined to that place.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00532

The Eternal Bride thus initiates Rûzbehân, her faithful lover, into a freedom from both incarnationism and idolatry, “filtering for him the pure draught of love, leaving in it not the slightest trace of an impure material mingling of divinity with humanity, yet softening the features of her sublimity so that a human being can bear her beauty, through that sweetly scented tinting to which the verse alludes: We created the human being in the most beautiful stature.” Rûzbehân says all this in incomparable language, not through abstractions, but through images that symbolically evoke his spiritual experience.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00533

The anonymous commentator is a remarkable ally to Rûzbehân’s insight, making explicit what lies behind his words. “Outwardly,” he says, “the case of the Faithful in Love resembles that of those among the Jews who associate (moshrikûn) another divinity with the One; it also resembles that of the Christian associators who have made Jesus and Maryam partners in divinity; and finally that of the Incarnationists in general (holâliyân), who professed that God dwells (enoikesis, immanence, holûl) within created beings.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00534

“Just as these three groups, after affirming divine oneness (tawhîd), were drawn toward dividing the divine nature or believing in incarnation, so the Faithful in Love, after attaining tawhîd in its purity, were troubled by the beauty of the human form and recognized signs of theophany (tajallî) in that form of manifestation (mazhar).
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00535

“But there is a difference. The former did not know what they were doing; unaware, they uttered absurdities. The Faithful in Love, however, became aware and saw: they explained and interpreted what their vision implied. The three expressions joined together by the venerable shaykh [Rûzbehân]—a draught filtered from this cup … despite the suspicion of incarnation … without the disturbance of any mingling of divinity and humanity—are three allusions meant to make clear the difference between the religion of love, on the one hand, and associationism and incarnationism on the other. Understand!”
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00536

This entire spirituality, then, rests upon the idea of theophany. Within Christian spirituality, one can speak of incarnatio continuata, a continuing incarnation, only figuratively, if the dogma of the Incarnation is maintained as a unique historical event. Theophanies, by contrast, are without limit, because the divine Attributes are without limit. With everything the idea entails—the mirror, the shâhid or witness of contemplation, the endless renewal of manifestation—theophany becomes the supreme pattern and governing principle of mystical experience.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00537

Rûzbehân explains: “When God, through love and inclination, makes his faithful servant both the Desiring and the Desired, both the Lover and the Beloved, that servant of love assumes toward God the role of witness of contemplation (shâhid). It is God who, in an eternal act of contemplation, contemplates himself within him and clothes him in his own Attributes. No incarnation takes place, for God remains apart from all created being. Or rather, here is something beyond the reach of understanding and intelligence.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00538

“Until you have understood what theophany is—God! God!—recite this precept: Shape your being according to the pattern of the divine qualities. When the divine lights have given his being a twofold significance [belonging to two orders at once], God invests him with the privilege of divine lordship (robûbîya). He becomes God’s beloved, for the divine intention toward this mystical lover is this: until in love you become identical with the Beloved, you cannot become one with the Beloved in the retreat where union is attained.”
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00539

In other words, divine love is the secret of theophany, and theophany is the very form that divine love takes. Until human love is shaped by that pattern, it has not attained perfection—which is to say, the divine reality of love—for that reality is theophany.
VI. The Inner Pilgrimage
passage-en-00540

But once this perfection has been reached, the one who contemplates is the one contemplated, and the lover is the beloved. This announcement of a transformation anticipates our final theme (see theme 6 below).
